text:
2.2 The HarborLink scenario
All examples in this lesson belong to one fictitious company: HarborLink.
HarborLink sells a subscription-based customer-communication platform to small and mid-sized businesses. A customer signs up for a monthly plan, receives invoices, pays them, writes to support, and sometimes complains. HarborLink staff record notes in a CRM. Finance staff monitor unpaid invoices.
The company is invented. Every customer name, email, invoice and identifier in the repository is synthetic. We use one coherent story so that the same people and amounts reappear in the CSV file, the Excel workbook, the JSON file, the database, the API and the PDF invoices.
The analytical question that motivates the lesson is simple:

Which customers have unpaid or overdue subscriptions, and what do we actually know about them?

Before we can answer that question with statistics or machine learning, we must obtain reliable structured data.

2.4 Part 1 — From real-world business information to structured data

2.4.1 Start with familiar business information
Do not start from file formats. Start from the information that professionals already meet at work.
Around 5 September 2026, HarborLink receives this email from Elena Vargas, customer 1827, who manages Atelier Vega:

“Hello, I am contacting you because my September subscription has still not been paid. Could you please check?”

A human reader understands the message immediately. The customer is worried about a payment. The month is September. The tone is polite. None of that is yet a statistical observation.
The same business event can leave several traces:








Everyday situation
Original information
What can become structured fields




A customer subscribes
Signed contract, welcome email, CRM form
Customer identifier, plan, amount, start date, country


An invoice is issued
PDF invoice, entry in the finance system
Invoice identifier, dates, amount, due date, status


A payment is overdue
Reminder letter, accounting status
Status, due date, days late, reminder date


A customer sends an email
The email itself
Date, channel, customer identifier, a short type, the text


A CRM note is typed
Free-text note
Author, date, customer, a coded category, the text


A ticket or complaint arrives
Support tool, email, phone summary
Ticket identifier, type, channel, status, text


A reminder is sent
Email or letter generated by a process
Date, template, invoice identifier, amount


An order is placed
Order form or ERP document
Order identifier, products, quantity, amount


A supplier invoice arrives
PDF or e-invoice from a supplier
Supplier, amount, account, due date



For each example, three layers should be kept apart:

The original business information — the email, the PDF, the CRM note, the ERP screen.
The structured fields that can be stored in a table — identifiers, dates, amounts, statuses, channels.
The information that may later be turned into numerical variables — for example a late-payment indicator, a text embedding, or a sentiment score.

The email above is not automatically a convenient row in a dataset. We can, however, represent the interaction as a structured record:

Read this table slowly.

customer_id, date, channel and status are structured fields. They can be filtered, counted and joined to other tables.
text preserves the original message. We do not throw the email away just because we have extracted a few fields.
amount does not appear in the email. The number 49.90 comes from another source: the September invoice in HarborLink’s finance records. A processing system that guessed “49.90” from the email alone would be inventing a value.
The structured record can be stored in a table and then loaded into Python.
The text itself may later be analysed with natural language processing or turned into a numerical representation. That is a later step, not the step we take now.

Three kinds of information are therefore mixed in any real extraction task:

Existing metadata — the email date, the sender, the customer identifier already known to the CRM.
Information explicitly present in the text — “September”, “subscription”, “not been paid”.
Information inferred by a processing system — interaction_type = payment_issue, or an amount copied from another system.

Do not pretend that every field can always be extracted perfectly from an email. Extraction creates hypotheses that often need validation.


2.4.2 Structured, semi-structured and unstructured data
These three labels are pedagogical simplifications. Real business data often sits on a continuum, and one document can contain both a clean table and a free-text comment. The labels remain useful if we treat them as a map, not as a law.

Structured data
Structured data is organised into well-defined fields and records. A row is an observation. A column is a variable.
Typical HarborLink examples:

a customer table;
a payment table;
an invoice table;
transaction records;
a spreadsheet whose columns are consistent from the first row to the last.

If finance exports a customer list with one row per customer and the same columns on every row, the export is structured.


Semi-structured data
Semi-structured data has organisation, but not necessarily the shape of a simple rectangle.
Typical examples:

JSON objects;
nested API responses;
application events;
logs;
records that contain lists or objects inside other objects.

A HarborLink interaction document may contain a customer identifier, a nested subscription object, and a list of contacts. That is structured enough to parse, but it is not yet one tidy table.


Unstructured or weakly structured information
Here the useful structure is not directly represented as a table.
Typical examples:

emails;
CRM notes;
complaints;
contracts;
PDF documents;
scanned invoices;
free-text customer-service tickets.

The HarborLink email is weakly structured: it has a sender and a date, but the meaning lives in the sentences. A scanned supplier invoice may look perfectly tabular to a human and still be only an image to a computer.



2.4.3 ERP systems as business information sources
An ERP — Enterprise Resource Planning — is an integrated business-management information system.
That sentence is easy to rush past, so we unpack it.

An ERP is not a file format. It is not “the SAP file” or “the Oracle CSV”.
An ERP is not necessarily one single database. It generally relies on databases, applications, business rules and interfaces.
It can manage information and processes such as finance, accounting, purchasing, sales, invoices, payments, inventory, suppliers and operations.

HarborLink might use an ERP to keep:

customer or business-partner information;
invoices;
payment records;
accounting information;
orders;
products or services;
suppliers;
operational transactions.

An analyst generally does not need, and should not automatically manipulate, the entire internal ERP data model. The usual objective is to obtain a relevant and authorised subset for a specific analytical task.
HarborLink wants to study late payments. The useful extracted subset might contain:

invoice identifier;
customer identifier;
invoice date;
due date;
amount;
payment status;
payment date;
order identifier.

That subset can then be transferred to an analytical system or loaded into Python. Everything else in the ERP — warehouse movements, supplier master data, posting rules — can remain untouched.


2.4.4 ERP extraction and analytical integration
Enterprises rarely ask a data scientist to click through ERP screens. They use automated mechanisms to extract data for statistical analysis and machine learning.
At a high level, the landscape includes:

manual or scheduled exports;
APIs;
ERP connectors;
ETL and ELT pipelines;
data integration platforms;
replication;
change data capture, where the product supports it;
data warehouses;
lakehouses;
analytical databases.

The conceptual path is stable even when the products change:

flowchart LR
    A[ERP source system] --> B[Extraction or integration]
    B --> C[Analytical data platform]
    C --> D[Python or another analytical tool]




flowchart LR
    A[ERP source system] --> B[Extraction or integration]
    B --> C[Analytical data platform]
    C --> D[Python or another analytical tool]






ETL means extract, transform, load: data are cleaned on the way to the analytical store. ELT means extract, load, transform: data land first, then they are transformed inside the analytical platform. Both patterns exist. The lesson does not require you to choose one.
The exact mechanism depends on the ERP product, the version and deployment model, the available interfaces, licences, authorisations, security policies and the company’s data architecture.
Direct access to the ERP’s internal database is not always available, and it is not always recommended. Production systems have business rules, audit trails and access controls. An unauthorised query can be a security incident as well as a technical mistake.


2.4.5 Examples of ERP systems
The objective of this subsection is awareness, not product training. Companies use integrated business systems. Those systems are important sources of analytical data. We are not learning to configure them.
Common examples include:

SAP, including SAP S/4HANA;
Oracle ERP / Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP;
Microsoft Dynamics 365;
Odoo.

Sage, Infor or NetSuite appear in the same landscape. A long catalogue is not useful here.

SAP as a concrete illustration
SAP is used here only as an illustration of enterprise extraction. The Python demonstrations do not require a SAP installation or access to any real ERP.
In relevant SAP environments, authorised users and integration tools can expose selected business data through views or interfaces. Names you may meet later in a company include:

CDS Views (Core Data Services Views) — defined views over business data, intended for consumption rather than for browsing internal tables;
SAP BW/4HANA — an analytical destination that can receive extracted data;
APIs and other integration interfaces;
full extraction or incremental / delta extraction, when the landscape supports it.

We will not teach ABAP, SAP configuration, SAP authorisations or the internal SAP data model. The diagram that matters is:

flowchart LR
    A[SAP or other ERP] --> B[Authorised interface or connector]
    B --> C[Selected business data]
    C --> D[Analytical platform or files]
    D --> E[Python / pandas]




flowchart LR
    A[SAP or other ERP] --> B[Authorised interface or connector]
    B --> C[Selected business data]
    C --> D[Analytical platform or files]
    D --> E[Python / pandas]






If HarborLink used SAP, the late-payment subset listed above would travel along that path. In this course, the same subset is already waiting for us as a small synthetic database and a few files.



2.4.6 CRM and other sources
A CRM — Customer Relationship Management — system is another major source of business information. It typically holds:

customer profiles;
customer interactions;
emails;
CRM notes;
sales opportunities;
customer-service tickets;
complaints;
reminders;
subscriptions;
contact history.

The conceptual distinction is:

ERP: broad business-management processes such as finance, accounting, purchasing, inventory and operations.
CRM: customer relationships, sales and customer interactions.

A real company often uses several systems at once. HarborLink’s unpaid invoice lives in the finance/ERP world. Elena Vargas’s email and the staff note live in the CRM world. A data scientist who studies late payments may need both: the amount and due date from finance, and the complaint or reminder history from the CRM.
Other sources sit beside these two systems: Excel files emailed by a colleague, a questionnaire, a web page, a PDF contract, a scanned document, or a JSON payload received through an API.


2.4.7 The distinctions that close Part 1
Keep these pairs separate. They are the conceptual backbone of the lesson.



Do not confuse
With




Business information
Structured data


Structured data
Numerical representation


Source system (ERP, CRM)
File format (CSV, JSON, PDF)


Extraction
Analysis


Extraction
Interpretation


Original text
Extracted metadata


Automatic extraction
Validated information



Conclusion of Part 1. Data science often begins before modelling. It begins by identifying where information exists, understanding its structure, obtaining authorised access to it, and converting it into reliable analytical data.

2.5 Part 2 — Loading and transforming data with Python
The rest of the lesson is practical. Every demonstration uses the HarborLink files in data/raw/.
The practical objective is:
Different sources and representations → Python → structured data → pandas DataFrame

2.5.1 What pandas is, and why we use it
A Python package is a reusable collection of functions and objects that we install once and then import into a program. pandas is the package most often used in Python to store and manipulate tables.
An import makes that package available in the current session.

import pandas as pd


import pandas loads the package.
as pd is a conventional short name. After this line, we write pd instead of pandas.
pd is not a special keyword. It is simply the name we chose to use.

A DataFrame is a rectangular in-memory table: rows and columns with labels. In this lesson:

a row is one observation — one customer, one invoice, one interaction, depending on the table;
a column is one variable — customer_id, monthly_amount, status, and so on.

A DataFrame is useful because statistical analysis and most machine-learning tools in Python expect data in this rectangular form. It is not a database. It lives in memory for the current session.


2.5.2 CSV: a tabular export
A CSV file (comma-separated values) is a plain-text representation of a table. Businesses use it constantly: finance exports, CRM extracts, reports sent by email.
HarborLink’s customer export is data/raw/customers.csv. It is a denormalised snapshot: each row already combines customer, subscription and current payment status. That is typical of the files analysts receive. It is not a full ERP model.

The argument "data/raw/customers.csv" is the path to the file, relative to the project root.

2.5.4 JSON: objects, lists and nested documents
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a format for representing structured or semi-structured information.
It is important to say what JSON is not:

JSON is not an API;
JSON is not a database;
JSON is not restricted to JavaScript.

Companies use JSON because software systems can produce and consume it easily. It appears in API responses, application events and integration files. It may be stored in a .json file or transmitted over a network.
The basic building blocks are:

an object: a collection of named fields, written with braces;
a key/value pair: "customer_id": 1827;
a list: an ordered collection, written with square brackets;
a nested object: an object stored inside another object;
a nested structure: lists and objects combined.

2.5.5 SQL and relational databases
A company uses a database rather than a single CSV file when several tables must stay consistent, when many users update the same records, or when the volume is larger than a convenient spreadsheet.
A relational database stores data in tables that can be linked.

a table is a named collection of rows;
a row is a record;
a column is a field;
a primary key uniquely identifies a row (customer_id in customers);
a foreign key points to a row in another table (customer_id in payments);
a relationship is that link;
a query asks for a subset;
filtering keeps some rows;
a join combines tables through their keys.

We use SQLite because it is a real relational database stored in one file. It does not require an external server. HarborLink’s file is data/raw/company.sqlite.

2.5.6 APIs: an interface, not a format
An API (Application Programming Interface) is an interface through which software can access data or services.
The distinction with JSON must stay explicit:

JSON is a format used to represent data.
An API is an interface used to request data or services.

An API may return JSON. It may also return XML, a file or an error message. The format and the interface are different ideas.
The conceptual pipeline is:

2.6 Part 3 — Extracting data from documents: the PDF problem
The files in Part 2 already had a logical structure: columns, keys, tables, JSON fields. Documents are different.

Extracting text from a document is not the same as reconstructing the structured information represented by that document.


2.6.1 Why PDF extraction is difficult
A PDF is primarily a document-preservation format. It is designed to keep a page looking the same on another computer, another printer, another year. It is not designed to keep a table as a table.
A layout that looks like rows and columns to a human may internally be a collection of text fragments placed at coordinates. The consequences are practical:

visual appearance and logical structure are different things;
text may be stored in separate fragments;
reading order may be ambiguous;
columns may be interleaved;
tables may have no explicit row or column metadata;
headers and footers may be mixed into the extracted text;
multi-column layouts may be read in the wrong order;
page breaks may split a table;
merged cells may be ambiguous;
a scanned PDF may contain only images.

HarborLink’s September invoice for Elena Vargas exists in two versions on purpose:

data/raw/invoice_text.pdf — a text-based invoice;
data/raw/invoice_scanned.pdf — a visually similar image-based invoice.

The business content is the same: invoice INV-2026-0901, customer 1827, premium subscription, 49.90 EUR, status unpaid. The encoding is not the same.


2.6.2 Text-based PDFs
A text-based PDF contains machine-readable characters. We can open it and ask a library for the text and, sometimes, for tables.
We use PyMuPDF, imported as pymupdf. It can open a file, count pages, extract text, list images and try to detect tables.

A scanned PDF may contain a photograph of a page rather than machine-readable text. Ordinary text extraction then returns little or nothing useful.

The scanned file looks like an invoice. Extraction finds an image and no usable text. The computer does not “see” 49.90 until another process turns the image into characters.
The conceptual chain for that other process is:
Scanned PDF → image → OCR → text → structuring → DataFrame
OCR (optical character recognition) is the step that guesses characters from pixels. It can be very useful. It can also misread a 5 as an S, invent a decimal, or skip a faded due date.
This lesson does not install an OCR engine. OCR typically needs extra system software and is not reliable enough to make a two-hour course depend on it. Treat the chain above as a concept you should know, not as a command you must run today.


2.6.4 Tables and complex layouts
Invoices, financial reports and contracts concentrate the difficulties:

tables that span several pages;
multiple columns of narrative text;
headers, footers and page numbers;
footnotes;
merged cells;
nested tables;
layouts that change from one month to the next.

Six jobs are often confused:

Extracting text.
Extracting geometric elements (boxes, lines, images).
Detecting tables.
Reconstructing rows and columns.
Interpreting the meaning of fields (49.90 is an amount; 1827 is a customer identifier).
Validating the extracted data against another source.

A library that succeeds at step 1 may still fail at step 4. A model that succeeds at step 5 may still be wrong at step 6.
Compare the PDF amount with the database. If they disagree, the document extraction is not finished.

2.6.5 Modern document-extraction approaches
The current landscape, at a high level, includes:

PDF parsers such as the one we just used;
OCR for image-based pages;
specialised table-extraction tools;
document AI systems;
cloud document-processing services;
extraction based on large language models or vision-language models.

Modern AI approaches can help interpret complex documents. They do not remove the need for:

validation;
consistency checks;
provenance (where did this number come from?);
human review when the decision matters;
confidentiality and security controls;
explicit checks of numerical values, dates and identifiers.

We will not implement a complete LLM pipeline in this lesson. An impressive extraction that cannot be checked is not analysis-ready data.


2.6.6 What the two PDFs were built to show
The text-based invoice contains real characters. The scanned invoice contains a picture of the same characters. Both were generated from the HarborLink scenario. If you open them side by side, they should look like ordinary business documents. The difference appears only when software tries to read them.
That is the PDF problem in one pair of files.

The difficulty is not merely reading characters. The challenge is recovering reliable structured information from a document whose layout and meaning may not be explicitly encoded.

3.3 The analytical unit is the invoice
The late-payment question is not “one row per customer” and not “one row per email”. The useful statistical unit is:

One row per invoice — one billing cycle for one customer.

That choice decides everything that follows. We start from the invoice table. Every other table is used only to add columns to those invoice rows. We never replace the invoice as the row.
If we later need one row per customer, we can aggregate this table. Starting too aggregated would throw away the monthly variation that plots will show.

3.4 What a merge actually does
A merge does not “blend two files together”. It walks along the invoice table, row by row, and looks up extra fields in another table.
Take Elena Vargas’s September invoice. After loading, that row already knows the invoice identifier, the customer identifier, the dates, the amount and the finance status. It does not yet know her name, her country, her plan, whether a payment arrived, or whether she emailed support.

3.16 Document the variables
Column names such as n_payment_issues or status_api are short for Python. Their meaning was not invented at the end of the join. Three commands carry the sentences from construction to Excel:

Collect — write_source_description_files (called by python/generate_analysis_data.py) writes one *_variables.csv next to each extract.
Forward — read_descriptions loads a companion; attach_descriptions copies selected rows onto the invoice catalog, with the same rename / keep / skip as the data joins.
Write Excel — write_variable_workbooks(data, descriptions, dictionary_path, summary_path) takes any data file and any description file and writes a dictionary workbook and a summary workbook.

The packaged forwarding step is forward_invoice_descriptions in python/harborlink_catalog.py. python/build_analysis_frame.py calls it when it rebuilds harborlink_invoices.csv, so the merged descriptions travel with the merged data even if you skip these cells.

It does not look up rows; it looks up column names. rename is the same mapping we used on the data (status → payment_status in the SQL, status → status_api for the API). keep copies only the columns that the join actually attached. skip avoids writing customer_id twice.
The CRM counts (n_interactions, …) and the analysis columns (days_to_due, …) never existed in a source file. Their descriptions are attached at the moment those columns are created, just as the numbers themselves are.

    crm_count_descriptions,
)

    descriptions,
    "data/raw/analysis/customers_variables.csv",
    skip=["customer_id"],
)
descriptions = attach_descriptions(
    descriptions,
    "data/raw/analysis/subscriptions_variables.csv",
    keep=["subscription_type", "monthly_amount", "start_date"],
)
descriptions = attach_descriptions(
    descriptions,
    "data/raw/analysis/payments_variables.csv",
    rename={"status": "payment_status"},
    keep=["payment_id", "payment_date", "payment_status"],
)
descriptions = attach_descriptions(descriptions, crm_count_descriptions())
descriptions = attach_descriptions(
    descriptions,
    "data/raw/analysis/api_invoices_variables.csv",
    rename={"status": "status_api"},
    keep=["status_api"],
)
descriptions = attach_descriptions(descriptions, analysis_column_descriptions())
descriptions.to_csv("data/processed/harborlink_invoices_variables.csv", index=False)

4.2 The HarborLink question
HarborLink still wants to understand late payments. Elena Vargas, customer 1827, has an unpaid September invoice of EUR 49.90. That is one case. Exploratory analysis asks what the table as a whole looks like.
Useful questions:

How many invoices are paid, unpaid or overdue?
Is non-payment concentrated in some plans, segments or countries?
How quickly do customers pay when they do pay?
Did something change over time, or is September special because it is the current month?
Do CRM messages tell us something we did not already know from the payment status?

is_outstanding is a Boolean: True when the payment is unpaid or overdue. The mean of a Boolean is the proportion of True. That is the outstanding rate.

invoices["payment_status"].value_counts()

payment_status
paid       3108
overdue     172
unpaid       45
Name: count, dtype: int64



invoices["is_outstanding"].mean()

np.float64(0.06526315789473684)


value_counts() counts rows in each category. About 3,100 invoices are paid. A little over 200 are not. The outstanding rate is about 6.5%. Counts and rates answer different questions: “how many problems do we have?” versus “how frequent is the problem?”
The three values of payment_status are a snapshot on 12 September 2026. They do not mean the same thing:







Status
What it means in this table




paid
A payment_date is recorded. That includes invoices paid after the due date. Late payment that was eventually recorded stays paid; it does not become overdue.


unpaid
No payment is recorded, and the due date has not yet passed. Here, all unpaid invoices are September invoices due on 15 September.


overdue
No payment is recorded, and the due date has already passed. There is no payment_date. overdue is not “paid late”; paid-late invoices are paid with paid_after_due = True.



So overdue means: as of the snapshot, this invoice was never recorded as paid. For a closed month, that is an invoice that remained without a payment.


4.3.3 Missing values are already an interpretation

invoices.isna().sum()[invoices.isna().sum() > 0]

customer_segment     116
payment_date         217
status_api          3085
days_to_pay          217
dtype: int64


Three missings matter, and they do not mean the same thing:

payment_date and days_to_pay are missing when there was no payment. That is the outcome we study, not a data accident.
status_api is missing for every invoice that is not in the September snapshot. The API does not cover history.
customer_segment is missing for 10 customers in the customer CSV (the same empty cells appear in the Excel customer sheet). Those 10 customers produce 116 invoice rows without a segment. The gap is in the customer file, not in the invoice file. Keep it as a category called unknown, rather than silently dropping the rows.


invoices["segment"] = invoices["customer_segment"].fillna("unknown")
invoices["segment"].value_counts()

segment
smb           1939
mid-market     892
enterprise     378
unknown        116
Name: count, dtype: int64


fillna("unknown") replaces missing segment labels by an explicit word. The invoices stay in the table. If we dropped them, we would hide a data-quality issue and slightly change the outstanding rate.


4.3.4 Matplotlib and seaborn, in one picture
A matplotlib figure is the whole image. An axes is the drawing area inside it: the panel that will contain the bars or points, with the scale marks and numbers along the sides (the ticks). Seaborn draws onto that axes. We will almost always write:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.someplot(..., ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("...")
ax.set_ylabel("...")
ax.set_title("...")

plt.subplots() creates the figure and one axes. It returns both; we store them in fig and ax.
Seaborn’s plotting functions have an argument also called ax. Writing ax=ax means: use our drawing area ax as the value of seaborn’s ax argument, so the plot is drawn on the figure we just created rather than on some other plot.
set_xlabel / set_ylabel name the axes in words a colleague can read.
The title should state the claim of the picture, not the command that produced it.



4.3.5 First graph: how many invoices in each payment status?
The first business question is simply: what is the current mix of statuses?

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.countplot(
    data=invoices,
    x="payment_status",
    order=["paid", "unpaid", "overdue"],
    ax=ax,
)
ax.set_xlabel("Payment status")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of invoices")
ax.set_title("Most invoices are paid; overdue is rarer than it feels in the CRM")
plt.show()




Number of HarborLink invoices by payment status.





sns.countplot counts rows.
data=invoices is the DataFrame.
x="payment_status" places the category on the horizontal axis. Each bar is one status.
order=[...] fixes the order. Without it, seaborn would follow the order of appearance in the file, which is not a story.

Interpretation. Paid invoices dominate. That is expected for a subscription business: most bills are collected. The operational attention sits in the two smaller bars. They are not interchangeable. Unpaid invoices are still inside the payment window. Overdue invoices are closed-cycle bills with no payment recorded in the table. A graph that lumped them together would mix “still waiting” with “still not paid after the due date”.
Invoices paid after the due date do not appear in the overdue bar. They remain paid. Elena’s September invoice belongs to the unpaid bar: her due date is 15 September and the extract is dated 12 September.

4.4.1 Do not plot a number before asking what it can be
amount looks numerical. A histogram is the reflex.

ax.set_xlabel("Invoice amount (EUR)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of invoices")
ax.set_title("Amount is not a smooth distribution: it is three catalogue prices")

Invoice amounts. The three spikes are the three HarborLink plans.





sns.histplot counts how many rows fall into intervals of x.
bins=20 asks for twenty intervals. The exact number is less important than the shape.

Interpretation. There are no amounts between the spikes. HarborLink does not bill “around 30 euros”. It bills starter 19.90, standard 29.90 and premium 49.90. A histogram was the wrong default. The honest graph is a bar of plans.

text:
5.1 Stage 1 — Define the business question
A telecommunications company wants to know which customers are likely to leave. Leaving is called customer churn. The company already stores a structured record for each customer: contract, services, tenure and charges, together with a label that says whether that customer churned. It also has written communications: complaints, billing messages, support conversations and internal notes.
This workshop is a guided investigation of one question.
Do the communications contain useful information beyond the structured customer record, once we judge the models on customers they did not see during fitting?
You will compare three approaches on the same test customers:
The model in all three cases is a logistic regression: a simple, standard way to turn customer information into a score between 0 and 1. We keep the model the same so that the comparison is about the information, not about a change of algorithm. A logistic regression is a good way to see a complete prediction workflow. It is not automatically the best model for every churn problem.
Three roles stay separate throughout the session.

text:
5.1.1 What churn means
Churn is the target. In this dataset it is a text field with two values: Yes if the customer left, and No if the customer stayed. A binary variable has two outcomes. The business question is richer than the label. The company would like a score for each customer, somewhere between 0 and 1, that ranks customers by how similar they are to historical customers who left.
A score is not yet a decision. A score of 0.80 does not, by itself, mean “call this customer” or “offer a discount.” The company still has to choose an action, a budget and a rule for how high a score must be before someone is contacted. That rule is called a cutoff.
Predicting a score is different from predicting only yes or no. The score can be sorted. The company can contact the 200 customers with the highest scores, or it can contact everyone above a cutoff. Those are business choices. The model supplies the ranking.


5.1.2 What information is available
Two files are used.
Dataset A, the customer table. This is the public Telco Customer Churn dataset published on Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/blastchar/telco-customer-churn. One row is one customer. The prepared file in this project is data/raw/telco/telco_customers.csv. It contains the public fields. The identifier is customerID. The target is Churn.

text:
5.3 Stage 3 — Build the first logistic regression on the tabular data

5.3.1 The idea, before the command
Historical customers have characteristics and a known outcome. A logistic regression looks for a weighted combination of those characteristics that separates, as well as a simple weighted sum can, the customers who left from the customers who stayed. For a new customer it turns that weighted sum into a score between 0 and 1.
Balanced class weights change the log-likelihood on the fit rows. Let n be the number of fit rows, n_leave the number who left, and n_stay the number who stayed. Each leaver is multiplied by n / (2 n_leave). Each stayer is multiplied by n / (2 n_stay). The weight of a row is 1 / (2 × the share of its own class). The two classes then have the same total weight. The fitted number is the score of that weighted fit.


5.3.2 One split, used for every model
Training data are the customers the model learns from. Test data are held out and used only to judge the result. If we judged the model on the customers it learned from, we would measure memory as well as prediction.
The split is stratified on Churn: the share of churners is kept similar in both groups. 
customerID is not a predictor. It names a person, and it would let a model memorize individuals rather than learn a pattern that applies to someone new. Churn is not a predictor. It is the answer.
Numeric fields are tenure, MonthlyCharges and TotalCharges. They are rescaled using the training customers only, then the same rescaling is applied to the test customers. A charge of 70 and a tenure of 70 are different facts; rescaling stops a field with large units from dominating for that reason alone.
Fields such as contract and payment method are categories. Each category (present in the training data) becomes a set of yes/no columns. The technical name is one-hot encoding.

TotalCharges and tenure describe related facts about the same history. The model may use both. That does not make each one a separate cause of churn.

Test recall is 0.797: at the current cutoff the model flags that share of the positive test rows. Accuracy and recall answer different questions. Accuracy alone is a weak guide when most rows are negative.


Accuracy is the share of test customers whose yes/no flag matches what actually happened. Recall is the share of churners the model flags. Precision is the share of flagged customers who really churned. F1 is a single compromise between precision and recall. It is convenient, and it hides the trade-off, so we still read precision and recall separately.
No one of these numbers describes the model.


5.4.2 Who was flagged
A confusion matrix crosses the actual outcome with the flag. The plain-language counts below are the test customers. In technical shorthand, flagged churners are true positives, flagged stayers are false positives, missed churners are false negatives, and unflagged stayers are true negatives.

A flag is a score at or above the cutoff. It is an input to a decision, and it is itself a decision only after the business accepts that cutoff.


If the company contacts every flagged customer, recall is the share of leavers it will find, and precision is the share of those contacts who were going to leave. The rest of the contacts are false alarms. Which of those is more expensive is a business question. The model does not answer it.


5.4.3 Ranking, across cutoffs
ROC-AUC measures how often a randomly chosen churner receives a higher score than a randomly chosen stayer. A value of 0.5 means the ranking is no better than chance. A value of 1 means every churner is ranked above every stayer. The curve shows that trade-off as the cutoff moves: the horizontal axis is the share of stayers who are flagged, and the vertical axis is the share of churners who are flagged.
PR-AUC uses the same ranking and reads the contact list. Order the customers from the highest score to the lowest. Pick a leaver at random, each leaver equally likely. Keep that leaver and every customer ranked at least as high. Customers with the same score are kept together. Precision is the share of this group who left. PR-AUC is the expected value of that share. A value of 1 means every leaver stands above every stayer, so the kept group contains only leavers. A ranking with no link to the outcome has PR-AUC equal to the share of leavers. This chapter judges the ranking by ROC-AUC, and one cutoff by precision and recall. Chapter 7 computes PR-AUC because its comparison table and the cloud evaluation both report it.

5.5 Stage 5 — Turn communications into numerical features

5.5.1 Why the model cannot read the notes directly
A logistic regression adds weighted fields. It cannot add the sentence “the line has been unreliable” to a monthly charge. We first turn each customer’s messages into numbers.
The existing procedure has three parts.

One document per customer. The customer’s messages are joined in text_index order. A customer with no messages would keep an empty document and would stay in the table.
TF-IDF, short for term frequency–inverse document frequency. Each word, and each two-word phrase, receives a score. The score is high when the expression is common in this customer’s document and uncommon across the other training documents. Very common English words are set aside.  The training step keeps up to 5,000 expressions.
LSA, latent semantic analysis. A compression method based on singular value decomposition (SVD) reduces those thousands of scores to k numbers, named text_1, text_2, and so on, up to text_k. Customers who use related wording end up with similar numbers. You do not need SVD to use the result. You do need to know that k is N_TEXT_COMPONENTS in the settings cell.

These columns are a numerical summary of patterns in the writing. They are not complaint counts, and they do not have business names such as “billing anger.”
The word list and the compression are learned from the training customers only. The same learned step is then applied to the test customers. If the test customers were allowed to influence the word list, information from the test set would leak into the model and the evaluation would look better than it is.

5.8.3 What a manager should ask before anyone uses a score
Return to the sentence you wrote in Stage 1. Then ask at least these questions.

Does the model improve performance on customers it did not see during fitting? The test rows are the evidence in this workshop. One split still leaves uncertainty.
Is any improvement large enough to pay for collecting, storing and processing the communications?
Are the scores reliable enough for the decision, or are they only a ranking? The average score and the cutoff discussion in Stage 4 are the start of that question, not the end of it.
What action follows a high score? A call, an offer, a service fix and a decision to do nothing are different actions with different costs.
Were the notes available before the outcome? This file has no message date, so it cannot answer that.
Did any field, including the wording of a note, already contain the outcome?
What has to be settled on data quality, privacy, fairness and operations before a score is allowed to change how customers are treated?

text:
6.1 Stage 1 — From churn prediction to an economic decision
A score ranks customers by how likely they are to leave. A retention campaign asks a further question.
Which customers should the company target so that the expected economic cost is as small as possible?
Targeting a customer costs money. It can also change the probability that the customer leaves. The decision uses the cost, the loss if the customer leaves, and both probabilities (to leave with or without the campaign).
Run the cells from top to bottom.
The previous workshop scored each test customer with a logistic regression that uses the structured fields and the communications. Those customers were not used to fit the model. This workshop treats that score as an input to a decision.
The scores are loaded from SCORE_FILE. They are not computed again. The previous workshop writes that file with save_scores. In the example, both workshops use data/processed/telco/test_probabilities_with_text.csv. For another dataset, set SCORE_FILE below to the path you used when saving, for example data/processed/mydata/scores.csv. The load uses that path.
For customer \(i\):
\(p_{0,i}\) and \(p_{1,i}\) are probabilities, so each one lies between 0 and 1. \(c_i\) and \(L_i\) are zero or positive. You can supply your own values. The telco file is only the working example.
The expected cost of a decision depends on the money at stake, not only on the churn probability.

section: 6.2 Stage 2 — The expected-cost problem
text:
6.2 Stage 2 — The expected-cost problem
If the company targets customer \(i\), it pays \(c_i\). The probability of churn is then \(p_{1,i}\), so the expected loss is \(L_i p_{1,i}\).
If the company does not target customer \(i\), it pays no contact cost. The probability of churn stays \(p_{0,i}\), so the expected loss is \(L_i p_{0,i}\).
One expression covers both choices:
\[
C_i(a_i) = c_i a_i + L_i\big[(1-a_i)p_{0,i} + a_i p_{1,i}\big].
\]
The first term is the contact cost. It is paid only when \(a_i = 1\). The expression in brackets is the probability of churn under the choice you made. Multiply it by \(L_i\) to get the expected loss.
The total expected cost is the sum over (test) customers:
\[
J(a_1,\ldots,a_n) = \sum_i C_i(a_i).
\]
The problem is:
\[
\text{minimize } J(a_1,\ldots,a_n)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
a_i \in \{0,1\}
\text{ for every customer } i.
\]
The solution is a list \(a^\star = (a_1^\star,\ldots,a_n^\star)\). Target customer \(i\) when \(a_i^\star = 1\). Do not target customer \(i\) when \(a_i^\star = 0\).
The total is a sum of separate customer costs, so the choice for one customer does not change the arithmetic for another. Compare the two options for each customer:

Expected cost with no campaign: \(L_i p_{0,i}\).
Expected cost with a campaign: \(c_i + L_i p_{1,i}\).

Target customer \(i\) when the second amount is smaller. Rearrangement gives the same rule:
\[
L_i(p_{0,i} - p_{1,i}) > c_i.
\]
\(L_i(p_{0,i} - p_{1,i})\) is the expected loss avoided by the campaign. Target customer \(i\) if the expected loss avoided exceeds the campaign cost.
The expected net benefit is that comparison, written as one number:
\[
b_i = L_i(p_{0,i} - p_{1,i}) - c_i.
\]
Target customer \(i\) when \(b_i > 0\).

6.4 Stage 4 — When the decision is a probability cutoff
Impose three extra restrictions:

\(c_i = c\) for every customer;
\(L_i = L\) for every customer;
\(p_{1,i} = (1-r)p_{0,i}\), with the same effectiveness \(r\) for every customer.

Then \(p_{0,i} - p_{1,i} = r p_{0,i}\), and the expected net benefit becomes
\[
b_i = r L p_{0,i} - c.
\]
Target customer \(i\) when \(b_i > 0\). With \(r\) and \(L\) positive, that is the same statement as
\[
p_{0,i} > \frac{c}{r L}.
\]
The cutoff is therefore
\[
t^\star = \frac{c}{r L}.
\]
\(t^\star\) is a consequence of the cost calculation. It appears only when the contact cost, the loss, and the campaign effectiveness are each the same for every customer. Outside those three restrictions, the rule remains the customer-level comparison in Stage 3.

section: 6.5 Stage 5 — A limited campaign budget
text:
6.5 Stage 5 — A limited campaign budget
A budget \(B\) limits total contact spending:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{minimize } &\sum_i \Big(c_i a_i + L_i\big[(1-a_i)p_{0,i} + a_i p_{1,i}\big]\Big) \\
\text{subject to } &\sum_i c_i a_i \le B, \\
&a_i \in \{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The expected cost of a plan can be rewritten as
\[
J(a) = \sum_i L_i p_{0,i} - \sum_i b_i a_i.
\]
The first sum is the expected cost of targeting nobody. It does not depend on the decision. Minimising \(J\) under the budget is therefore the same problem as maximising the total expected net benefit, \(\sum_i b_i a_i\), under the same budget.
A customer with \(b_i \le 0\) is never selected. Targeting that customer would raise expected cost, and it would use budget.

6.5.1 Equal contact costs
Suppose every contact costs the same amount \(c\), and \(c > 0\). The budget can pay for at most
\[
K = \lfloor B / c \rfloor
\]
customers. The solution is then the \(K\) customers with the largest positive expected net benefits. If fewer than \(K\) customers have a positive benefit, target only those.
The cell below keeps the simulated campaign probabilities, so effectiveness still differs across customers. The contact cost is 40 and the loss is 600 for every customer. The budget pays for at most 200 contacts.

section: 6.7 Stage 7 — Campaign probabilities from real campaign data
text:
6.7 Stage 7 — Campaign probabilities from real campaign data
\(p_{1,i}\) was supplied to this workshop. A real campaign file would have to produce it.
A model fitted on customers who were offered the campaign can estimate the churn probability under the campaign, for customers who look like them.
That estimate is not yet the effect of the campaign. The effect is the difference between the outcome with the campaign and the outcome that would have occurred without it.
A randomized control group provides the comparison. Customers who were not offered the campaign identify \(p_{0,i}\). Customers who were offered it identify \(p_{1,i}\). Under a properly run randomization, the difference is the causal effect of the campaign.
A file that contains only customers who received the campaign does not identify what they would have done without it.
The telco file has no campaign indicator and no random assignment. It cannot estimate campaign effectiveness.
Uplift is the name for the difference in probabilities:
\[
u_i = p_{0,i} - p_{1,i}.
\]
The expected net benefit is then
\[
b_i = L_i u_i - c_i.
\]
The first customer to consider is the one with the highest positive expected net benefit. The budget decides whether that customer is affordable, and which affordable group has the largest total benefit. A high churn probability does not settle the choice. This workshop does not fit an uplift model.

section: 6.8 Test customers, and customers the model has already seen
text:
6.8 Test customers, and customers the model has already seen
The scores in this workshop are the test customers from the previous one. The model did not use those rows when it chose the coefficients. They stand in for customers the model has not seen.
They are still a slice of the same historical file. The churn on those rows has already happened. They are a stand-in for a current book, not the current book itself.
The same coefficients can be applied to every row of the file, including the rows that were used to fit the model. That produces a score for the whole file.

On a customer the model did not see, the score is the kind of number the test set is meant to give. The outcome did not help choose the coefficients.
On a customer who was used to fit the model, the outcome did help choose the coefficients. The score is pulled toward a result the model has already seen. It will look more accurate than a score on a new customer.

The observed outcome splits in the same way. On the test rows, it was not used to choose the coefficients. On the training rows, it was. Using those training rows as a check of the score mixes the past fit with the customers still to be decided about.
Keep the two groups apart. Fit on the past. Score the customers you might contact now. When the only available file is the historical one, use the test rows as the campaign table and leave the training rows out of it.

7.3 Gemini
Gemini, in this lesson, is the tabular AutoML service on Google Cloud. In the console the menu is Vertex AI. Some pages say Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The Python package is google-cloud-aiplatform. It is not the chat model.
You send fit_table. The service searches among model types and keeps one model. You then send the comparison rows, with no target. It returns a probability that the row has the positive label. In the example that label is Yes in Churn: the customer left. That probability is written back into validation_probabilities.csv.

7.3.1 Account, project, and bill
Do this in the browser before the training cell.

Open https://console.cloud.google.com/ and sign in.
Open https://console.cloud.google.com/projectcreate. Create a project. Copy the project ID. It is not the display name.
Open https://console.cloud.google.com/billing. Link a billing account to the project. Read the credit that remains.
Open https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/pricing. Read the tabular AutoML training price and the batch prediction price for the region you will set below.

Project. The container for the job, the files, and the bill.
Billing account. Training is refused until one is linked.
Region. The group of data centers. This lesson uses us-central1. The stored files and the job use the same region.


7.3.2 The API
An API is the list of requests a program may send. The requests used here are: store this table, train a classification model, score this other table, delete what was created.

Enable the two APIs. Enabling them does not upload customers and does not train.

Vertex AI API: https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/aiplatform.googleapis.com
Cloud Storage API: https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/storage.googleapis.com

Install the packages once, from the project folder, when you have decided to run a paid job.

source .venv/bin/activate
pip install google-cloud-aiplatform google-cloud-storage
On Windows, activate with .venv\Scripts\activate. Reading the saved comparison does not need these packages.
google-cloud-aiplatform is the Python client for Vertex AI. run_cloud() uses it to create the dataset, start the training job, and start the batch prediction. google-cloud-storage is the Python client for the bucket. run_cloud() uses it to upload the training CSV and to download the score file. Installing the packages does not upload a table and does not start a job. The bucket itself is created later, with the gcloud storage buckets create command.

Sign in from the terminal in the next section. Do not put a key file in this project folder.



7.3.3 Quantities the job reads
BUDGET_MILLI_NODE_HOURS is the training cap, in milli node hours. A node is one machine Google starts for the search, then stops. A node hour is that machine working for one hour. 1000 milli node hours = 1 node hour. 1000 is the smallest cap the service accepts. This lesson also refuses a value above 72000. The cap is the maximum machine-time of the search. The search keeps the best model found inside the cap. It is not a memory size. Scoring the comparison rows is a second machine and is not part of this number.
PLATFORM_VALIDATE_FRACTION = 0.10 and PLATFORM_TEST_FRACTION = 0.10 label the fit rows only. Gemini requires a column ml_split with the labels TRAIN, VALIDATE and TEST. Ten percent of the fit rows are VALIDATE, ten percent are TEST, and the rest are TRAIN. 
These labels are not test_table.
OPTIMIZATION_OBJECTIVE = "minimize-log-loss" tells the search to prefer probabilities that match OBSERVED_COLUMN.
SPLIT_COLUMN is the column this lesson adds to each training file. The service reads it. The labels are TRAIN, VALIDATE and TEST. It is not a predictor. The example name is ml_split.
GCS_PREFIX is the first folder inside the bucket. It is not a column of the table, and it is not a model. The example is telco-automl. One run writes its files under that folder, then under a timestamp. Set another prefix when a second dataset should not share the first dataset’s folder.
INCLUDE_TEXT_ONLY = False leaves out a third model that would use TEXT_FEATURE alone. True adds one more cap and a column p_automl_text_only. In the example TEXT_FEATURE is customer_text.
BUDGET = 8000 is the campaign budget from Chapter 6, in the same unit as cost. It is not the training cap.
manifest.json is a local file in OUTPUT_DIR. It is the record of the upload. It is not the training table. build_gemini_files(..., write=True) writes it. write=False leaves the file as it is.

7.3.5 What is billed
Three cloud objects appear after a search. Only one of them holds the fitted parameters.
Training pipeline. The search itself. It tries model types until the cap, or until early stopping. It is billed in node hours, up to BUDGET_MILLI_NODE_HOURS for each experiment. It does not keep a machine after it finishes.
Model. The registry entry written when the pipeline reaches PIPELINE_STATE_SUCCEEDED. This entry holds the fitted parameters: the chosen model and the numbers that turn a row into a probability of leaving. It is not a running computer. An entry that is only stored is not billed as a prediction machine.
Batch prediction. A machine that starts, loads that same registry entry, scores the comparison file, writes the score file into the bucket, and stops. The bill is the time that machine runs. This is the scoring step this lesson uses.
Endpoint. A second way to use the same registry entry. Deployment means loading the saved model onto a machine that stays on and answers one request at a time. The bill is the hours from that deployment until undeploy, which takes the model off the machine and stops the hourly charge. This lesson does not create an endpoint and does not deploy.
The fitted parameters stay in the model registry. The endpoint and the batch job are only machines that load those parameters. The endpoint is for repeated single requests. The batch job is for one file. The comparison needs one file, so the lesson builds a batch job and does not build an endpoint.
Bucket. A named folder on Google’s disks. The training CSV is copied there. The scores are written there, then copied back.
Prefix. The path of this lesson’s files inside the bucket. GCS_PREFIX is only the first folder. You set it in Quantities the job reads. In the example it is telco-automl. The bucket name is BUCKET. A run then adds its own timestamp, and each experiment adds its own file. The prefix is not a model and it is not a separate charge. The charge is the storage of the files under that path.

Node hour. Defined above. Each of the two searches is capped at BUDGET_MILLI_NODE_HOURS. Each search is followed by one batch prediction. A cancelled job is billed for the machine-time already used. Another training failure is not billed.
The prediction price list has a standard virtual machine and a Spot virtual machine for the same machine type: https://cloud.google.com/products/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/pricing#prediction-and-explanation. A virtual machine is one computer. A Spot virtual machine is spare capacity, so its hourly price on that page is the lower one. Google can take a Spot machine back. That interruption is preemption. The preempted time is not billed.
This lesson does not request a Spot machine. The training search is billed as AutoML node hours, up to the cap. It is not a virtual machine you choose on that page. Scoring uses one standard machine, and only after a model exists.
The search has no pause. PIPELINE_STATE_RUNNING means it continues with no further command. PIPELINE_STATE_SUCCEEDED means the model is saved. PIPELINE_STATE_CANCELLED means the search was stopped. A cancelled or failed search does not continue later. Another search is a new training pipeline, from the beginning. The partial search is not handed to another machine.
A Spot machine is useful when the lower hourly price still wins after some jobs are started again, and when you can wait. Custom training that writes a checkpoint can continue from that checkpoint on the next machine. A short scoring job can be cheaper on Spot even if a preempted job has to start again, because the preempted time is not billed.
That is not this lesson. The AutoML search does not give you a checkpoint to pass to a replacement machine. If it is stopped, the next search starts over. A preempted scoring job also starts over: the replacement machine does not receive the unfinished score file as a place to continue. The saved model stays, so scoring starts again and the search does not. For these two tasks, a partial result is not reused. Spot would only change the price of a job that may have to be launched again.

7.3.10 Compare the scores
Accuracy, precision and recall use DECISION_THRESHOLD. ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, log-loss and the Brier score do not. They use OBSERVED_COLUMN and the score column. ROC-AUC and PR-AUC describe the ranking. Log-loss, the Brier score and the calibration plot describe the probabilities. The campaign calculation uses the probability. In the example, OBSERVED_COLUMN is observed_outcome and 1 means the customer left.
In Chapter 5, under The idea, before the command, each fit row is weighted in the log-likelihood by 1 / (2 × the share of its own class). Leavers are fewer, so each leaver has the larger weight, and the two classes have the same total weight. The Gemini models fit without those weights. On the calibration plot, the logistic curve and the Gemini curve are scores from those two fits.
PR-AUC. Chapter 5, under Ranking, across cutoffs, defines ROC-AUC as the probability that a random leaver receives a higher score than a random stayer. That is one leaver compared with one stayer. PR-AUC reads the list those scores produce. Order the comparison customers from the highest score to the lowest. Pick a leaver at random, each leaver equally likely. Keep that leaver and every customer ranked at least as high. Customers with the same score are kept together. Precision at that leaver is the share of the kept group who left. PR-AUC is the expected value of that precision. It is the area under the precision-recall curve: as the cutoff moves, recall is the share of leavers who are kept, and precision is the share of the kept group who left. A value of 1 means the kept group contains only leavers, whichever leaver is chosen. A ranking with no link to the outcome has PR-AUC equal to the share of leavers in the comparison rows. ROC-AUC can stand well above one half while this expected precision stays near that share, because many stayers can still sit above a leaver. The column PR-AUC in the next table is this average.

A cohort with a different churn share, different losses, or a different effect of a contact need not repeat that overlap. The Chapter 6 rule is then applied again, to new scores and to the new costs. p1 remains an assumption. The realized net benefit accounts for these historical outcomes under that assumption. It compares the contact lists on this cohort. It is not a measured effect of a campaign, and it is not a forecast for a cohort that does not look like this one.
